items.title: 6.2.1 Equation of Tangent to a Circle

source_refs.note: Book p. 174-175: 6.2.1 (a) tangent to x^2 + y^2 = r^2, (b) tangent to the general circle, derived by implicit differentiation

blocks.text: (a) Circle centered at origin: x² + y² = r²

Let \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) be a point on the circle
\[x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2} \quad \text{...(i)}\]
Differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to \(x\), we have:
\[2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is implicit differentiation: \(y\) is a function of \(x\) on the circle, so the derivative of \(y^{2}\) is \(2y\frac{dy}{dx}\) (chain rule), and the derivative of the constant \(r^{2}\) is 0.
We do not need to solve for \(y\) first; differentiating the equation as it stands is quicker and works for the upper and lower halves of the circle at once.

The slope of the tangent at \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) is the value of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at this point:
\[m_{T} = \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_{1},\, y_{1})} = -\dfrac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}\]
Therefore, the equation of the tangent at \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) is:
\[y - y_{1} = -\dfrac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}(x - x_{1}), \quad y_{1} \ne 0\]
\[xx_{1} + yy_{1} = x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} \quad \text{...(ii)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The small step the book leaves out: multiply both sides by \(y_{1}\):
\[y_{1}(y - y_{1}) = -x_{1}(x - x_{1})\]
\[yy_{1} - y_{1}^{2} = -xx_{1} + x_{1}^{2}\]
Now take \(xx_{1}\) to the left and \(y_{1}^{2}\) to the right; this gives (ii).

Since \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) lies on the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}\), we have
\[x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} = r^{2} \quad \text{...(iii)}\]
From equations (ii) and (iii), we obtain the required equation of the tangent:

blocks.text_alt: x times x1 plus y times y1 equals r squared

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the condition \(y_{1} \ne 0\)? At the points \((\pm r, 0)\) the slope \(-\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}\) does not exist: the tangent there is vertical. The final formula still works: at \((r, 0)\) it gives \(x \cdot r = r^{2}\), that is \(x = r\), which is exactly the vertical tangent. So the final form \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} = r^{2}\) holds at every point of the circle.
Geometric check: the radius from \(O\) to \(P\) has slope \(\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}}\), and \(\frac{y_{1}}{x_{1}} \times \left(-\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}\right) = -1\). The tangent is perpendicular to the radius, as it must be.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration (not from the book): tangent to \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 25\) at \((3, 4)\).
First check the point is on the circle: \(9 + 16 = 25\).
\[3x + 4y = 25\]
Its slope is \(-\frac{3}{4}\), and the radius \(OP\) has slope \(\frac{4}{3}\); the product is \(-1\).

Let \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) be a point on the circle
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\]
Differentiating both sides with respect to \(x\):
\[2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2g + 2f\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\]
\[2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2f\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -2x - 2g\]
\[2(y + f)\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -2(x + g)\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x + g}{y + f}\]
The slope of the tangent at \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) is:
\[m_{T} = \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_{(x_{1},\, y_{1})} = -\dfrac{x_{1} + g}{y_{1} + f}\]
Hence, the equation of the tangent is:
\[y - y_{1} = -\dfrac{x_{1} + g}{y_{1} + f}(x - x_{1})\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Read the slope geometrically: the centre is \(C(-g, -f)\), so the radius \(CP\) has slope \(\frac{y_{1} + f}{x_{1} + g}\). The tangent's slope \(-\frac{x_{1} + g}{y_{1} + f}\) is its negative reciprocal. Again: tangent perpendicular to radius.

Multiplying both sides by \((y_{1} + f)\):
\[(y - y_{1})(y_{1} + f) = -(x_{1} + g)(x - x_{1})\]
\[yy_{1} + fy - y_{1}^{2} - fy_{1}\]
\[= -xx_{1} + x_{1}^{2} - gx + gx_{1}\]
Rearranging:
\[xx_{1} + yy_{1} + gx + fy\]
\[= x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + gx_{1} + fy_{1}\]
Adding \(gx_{1} + fy_{1}\) to both sides:
\[xx_{1} + yy_{1} + gx + gx_{1} + fy + fy_{1}\]
\[= x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} \quad \text{...(3)}\]
Since \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) lies on the circle, we have:
\[x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} + c = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} = -c \quad \text{...(4)}\]
Substituting equation (4) into equation (3) and rearranging gives the required equation:

blocks.text_alt: x x1 plus y y1 plus g times (x plus x1) plus f times (y plus y1) plus c equals 0

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why add \(gx_{1} + fy_{1}\)? Because it makes the right side exactly the left side of the circle's equation at \(P\) (without \(c\)), which we know equals \(-c\). This trick removes \(x_{1}^{2}\) and \(y_{1}^{2}\) and leaves a neat formula.
Like part (a), the final formula also covers the case \(y_{1} + f = 0\), where the tangent is vertical and the slope form cannot be used.
Put \(g = f = 0\) and \(c = -r^{2}\): the formula becomes \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} - r^{2} = 0\), which is part (a). So (a) is a special case of (b).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}\): tangent at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) is \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} = r^{2}\).
2. Circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\): tangent at \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) is \(xx_{1} + yy_{1} + g(x + x_{1}) + f(y + y_{1}) + c = 0\).
3. Both come from implicit differentiation and the point-slope form; the condition that \(P\) lies on the circle simplifies the result.
4. The tangent is always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using these formulas for a point that is not on the circle. First check that \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) satisfies the circle's equation.
2. Writing \(2g(x + x_{1})\) instead of \(g(x + x_{1})\): the 2 is already used up by the \(x + x_{1}\).
3. Applying the formula when the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are not 1. Divide the equation by that coefficient first.
